metadata.title: Simpson’s Paradox: When the Overall Trend Tells the Wrong Story
metadata.historical_scope: Standalone educational explainer; hypothetical marketing example only.
metadata.methodological_boundary: Both aggregate and subgroup statistics can be correct; Simpson’s Paradox does not automatically imply confounding or establish causal truth.
metadata.production_gate: Narrative and visual plan approved; review rendering authorized; clean final master not authorized.

beats.narration_text: What if the overall data says Campaign A performs better, but within every important customer group, Campaign B actually performs better? That sounds impossible. But both conclusions can come from correctly calculated data. The difference is hidden in how the populations are combined.

Consider a hypothetical marketing example. Across all customers, Campaign A converts sixty-eight percent, while Campaign B converts forty-two percent. Looking only at this aggregate KPI, Campaign A appears to be the obvious winner. But that comparison leaves out an important part of the story.

shot.visual_intent: Aggregate campaign conversion bars with hypothetical label.

beats.narration_text: The campaigns reached very different customer populations. Campaign A was shown mostly to high-intent customers, while Campaign B was shown mostly to low-intent customers. Those groups begin with different propensities to convert, before we even compare campaign performance.

shot.visual_intent: Different high- and low-intent audience proportions.

beats.narration_text: Now separate the results. Among high-intent customers, Campaign A converts eighty percent and Campaign B converts ninety percent. Within this group, Campaign B performs better. These are illustrative values for this hypothetical example, not results from a research study.

The low-intent group tells the same story. Campaign A converts twenty percent, while Campaign B converts thirty percent. Campaign B also performs better here. So B leads within both meaningful customer segments, even though A leads when every customer is aggregated.

The apparent conclusion has reversed. Overall, A looks stronger. Within high-intent customers, B is stronger. Within low-intent customers, B is stronger again. The arithmetic is not broken. The aggregate rates and subgroup rates are each calculated correctly.

This is Simpson’s Paradox: a pattern where a trend observed in aggregated data changes, disappears, or reverses after the data is divided into meaningful groups. A complete reversal is the most striking version, but a trend can also weaken or vanish.

Why does it happen here? Campaign A received a much larger proportion of high-intent customers, who were easier to convert under either campaign. Campaign B received mostly low-intent customers, who were harder to convert. The population mix pulled A’s overall average upward and B’s downward.

shot.visual_intent: Population composition blocks explain weighted aggregate result.

beats.narration_text: Customer intent matters because it is related to the composition of each campaign’s audience and to the outcome being measured: conversion. This can create a composition effect and may signal confounding. But Simpson’s Paradox alone does not prove a specific confounder or establish causality.

shot.visual_intent: Simple grouping-variable relationship diagram with causal guardrail.

beats.narration_text: Both statistical views can be mathematically correct because they answer different questions. The aggregate comparison weights the segments according to each campaign’s actual audience mix. The subgroup comparison asks how the campaigns differ among customers with similar intent. Interpretation depends on which question supports the decision.

shot.visual_intent: Both-correct comparison with different weighting and questions.

beats.narration_text: This matters far beyond marketing. Population composition can complicate healthcare comparisons, hiring metrics, product experiments, regional sales performance, and customer behavior analysis. Whenever groups differ in their baseline outcomes and are unevenly distributed, an aggregate KPI can hide important structure.

shot.visual_intent: Application grid across six analytics domains.

beats.narration_text: Simpson’s Paradox is not necessarily a calculation mistake or deliberate data manipulation. It does not mean aggregate metrics are always bad. And subgroup analysis does not automatically reveal causal truth. Selection, measurement, sample size, and the decision context still require careful examination.

Before acting on an aggregate KPI, ask five questions. Which populations were combined? Do the groups have different baseline outcomes? Were the options exposed to different group proportions? Does the pattern persist within meaningful groups? And which comparison actually answers the decision you need to make?

Aggregate statistics can be correct and still mislead interpretation when population composition is hidden. Subgroup statistics can reveal the hidden pattern, but they still require thoughtful analysis rather than automatic causal conclusions. Always ask what happens when the data is broken into the groups that actually matter. I’m Ushasvi Rachel with Humanitarians dot A I.
